newsitem.title: BOSNIA: FEATURE - Bosnian Moslems, Croats languish under Dayton.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bosnian Moslems, Croats languish under Dayton.

text.p: Pine-forested ridgelines dusted with snow loom above the mountain hollow known as Stupni Do, a Moslem village in central Bosnia obliterated by Croat forces in October 1993.
Fire-scorched foundations, rotting walls without roofs, rusted hulks of cars and the gurgle of water from unattended troughs and broken pipes greet the visitor.
Sixty-six houses were destroyed and 38 people massacred in a single morning here.
Beneath the floor of one deserted shell is the crawl-space where three women, discovered hiding that day, were executed.
Reporters later found the victims huddled together, their heads and shoulders protruding from a trap door.
There is the barnyard where incinerated cattle, legs stuck straight up, steamed in the chill air after the slaughter.
Not far away lay a human body, naked and charred black, which some animal had gnawed on, exposing pink flesh.
Standing amidst the desolation and the memories, the promise of the Dayton peace agreement is nowhere to be found. Reconstruction and reconciliation seem like whispered taunts.

Eight male Moslem survivors are gathered behind one ruin distilling the potent plum brandy, slivovitz. Smells of wood smoke and alcohol mingle as the men work copper kettles and tubing with practised ease.
"This is the first time we've made slivovitz since 1993. The plums were good that fall and we made some fine brandy before they burned our houses," explained Fadil Likic, 43.
"We lost everything and we have nothing. There's no money to rebuild. We have no jobs. We live off humanitarian aid. We climb up to the village as often as we can but there's no way to live here."
In the valley below one can glimpse the town of Vares, where these Moslem men now live in uneasy proximity to Croats, who were the pre-war majority in this area.
Now the Moslems, about 10,000 of them, predominate over an estimated 3,300 Croats and 70 Serbs.
Mato Topic is the Catholic priest in town, a man who spent virtually all of the 43-month Bosnian war in Vares ministering not just to his parishoners but to Serbs and Moslems as well.
"In many of its details the Dayton agreement has not been realised at all," he said.

"In this municipality no local government has been formed and therefore we are receiving no international aid. Across Bosnia those who attained power by force and ethnic cleansing are still in power. Nothing is new."
The priest speaks of incidents and provocations between Moslems and Croats. He brings out photographs of Catholic cemeteries vandalised -- headstones overturned and defaced.
The wooden fence around St. Michael's in Vares, Bosnia's oldest Catholic church, has been knocked down the night before.
"The problem is not these incidents," the priest explained.

"The problem is the power structure which does not try to find or punish the perpetrators. There is no war but there is a growing sense of lawlessness. Ordinary people are the victims. Here the Croats suffer, elsewhere it is Moslems."
Topic fumes over the troubles of local Catholics but is quick to point out that Moslems are denied justice too.
The Croat gang-leader who carried out the Stupni Do massacre of Moslems, Ivica Rajic, a man indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal, remains at large in Bosnia.
He lives not in hiding, but openly, and is spotted occasionally by journalists and aid workers.
Neither Croat authorities in areas where he resides and travels nor the 50,000 NATO troops in Bosnia have managed to arrest him or most of 75 other indicted war criminals.
"The whole world knows the crime committed at Stupni Do was carried out by Ivica Rajic. Every side has extremists but the authorities wink and let them go," the priest said.
"Rajic carried out the operation. He's a criminal and there can't be any peace here until he is brought to justice."
A year after Dayton was signed the problems in Vares and neighbouring Stupni Do are a reflection of the unresolved tensions within Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation.
The problems between Moslems and Croats mirror those which exist between their Federation and the Serb republic, which controls the other 49 per cent of Bosnia.
Nationalist parties rule the country with an iron hand, making a joke of ethnic reconciliation. Refugee returns are blocked, jobs are scarce.
The iron mine around which Vares revolved for centuries is closed and its factories are idle. Most of the town's dingy shop windows are empty. Up the hill, Stupni Do moulders in ruins.

Standing by a copper pot of bubbling plums near where his wife and other members of his family were massacred in 1993, 58-year-old Tahir Likic sips slivovitz and broods on the lessons of war and peace in Bosnia.
"Say what you will, before the war we had a good life together. It didn't matter whether you were Moslem or Serb or Croat, you could go where you wanted," the man explained.
"Now we have promises from Dayton and we have slivovitz and that's all we have."
